case_name: McGill University Health Centre (MUHC) c. O.B.
text:
McGill University Health
Centre (MUHC) c. O.B.

2017 QCCS 1786

JG 1462

SUPERIOR COURT

(Civil Division)

CANADA

PROVINCE OF QUÉBEC

DISTRICT OF

MONTRÉAL

No:

500-17-098434-171

DATE:

May 4, 2017

______________________________________________________________________

PRESENT: THE HONOURABLE PIERRE-C.
GAGNON, J.S.C.

______________________________________________________________________

McGILL UNIVERSITY HEALTH
CENTRE (MUHC)

and

EWA SIDOROWICZ

Applicants

v.

O. B.

Respondent

and

G. B.

Impleaded party

______________________________________________________________________

JUDGMENT ON AN
APPLICATION FOR AN AUTHORIZATION OF TREATMENT

______________________________________________________________________

A.

PRELIMINARY COMMENTS

[
1
]

Clearly, the respondent O. B. requires a
well-designed and well-administered treatment program for his schizoaffective
disorder, of a bipolar type.

[
2
]

But, in itself, the preceding statement is
insufficient to empower the Court to deprive Mr. B. of his fundamental rights
to autonomy and self-determination. For this to be decided, a high standard
must be met, as discussed below.

[
3
]

The Court was impressed of the testimony by the
father of O. B. (“Mr. B. Senior”), with the apparent approval of the mother,
also present in the courtroom for the duration of the hearing.

[
4
]

Mr. B.’s parents obviously love their son and
are concerned about his well-being and his capacity to remain involved in the
community.

[
5
]

The love and care of the parents are certainly
part of what Mr. B. requires to get well and remain well.

[
6
]

Mr. B. Senior urged the Court to mediate and
find some middle ground between what the Health Centre requires and what his
son is seeking. Mr. B. Senior insisted that a positive therapeutic alliance
between psychiatrist and patient, is preferable here to energetic coercion.

[
7
]

Mr. B. Senior did not agree to the treatment
program on behalf of his son.

B.

LEGAL RULES APPLICABLE

[
8
]

The cardinal rule is stated by the Québec
legislator at
Article 16
of the
Civil Code of Québec

(the “CCQ”):

Art. 16.
L’autorisation du tribunal est nécessaire en cas
d’empêchement ou de refus injustifié de celui qui peut consentir à des soins
requis par l’état de santé d’un mineur ou d’un majeur inapte à donner son
consentement; elle l’est également si
le majeur inapte à consentir refuse
catégoriquement de recevoir les soins
, à moins qu’il ne s’agisse de soins
d’hygiène ou d’un cas d’urgence.

Elle est, enfin, nécessaire pour soumettre un mineur âgé de 14 ans et
plus à des soins qu’il refuse, à moins qu’il n’y ait urgence et que sa vie ne
soit en danger ou son intégrité menacée, auquel cas le consentement du
titulaire de l’autorité parentale ou du tuteur suffit.

Art. 16.
The authorization of the
court is necessary where the person who may give consent to care required by
the state of health of a minor or a person of full age who is incapable of
giving his consent is prevented from doing so or, without justification,
refuses to do so; it is also necessary where
a person of full age who is
incapable of giving his consent categorically refuses to receive care
,
except in the case of hygienic care or emergency.

The authorization of the
court is necessary, furthermore, to submit a minor 14 years of age or over to
care which he refuses, except in the case of emergency if his life is in
danger or his integrity threatened, in which case the consent of the person
having parental authority or the tutor is sufficient.

[emphasis added by the Court)

[
9
]

The Court of Appeal has designed in the case of
G.
(A)
[1]

and more recently in the case of
F.D.
,
[2]

the test to be applied when it is alleged that a person of full age
categorically refuses to receive care, as alleged in the case of Mr. B.:

•

two essential conditions must be proven to
establish the material jurisdiction of the Court to seize itself of the
dispute:

(a)

the person’s incapacity to consent; and

(b)

the person’s
categorical
refusal.

•

to verify the person’s incapacity to consent,
the Court must consider five inter-related questions?

(a)  does the person understand the nature of the
illness for which a treatment is proposed?

(b)     does the person understand the nature and the
goal of the treatment?

(c)   does the person understand the advantages of the
treatment as well as the risks (if it is administered)?

(d)  does the person understand the risks involved (if
the treatment is not administered)?

(e)

does the illness affect the person’s capacity to understand and
decide?

[
10
]

In
G.(A),
[3]

the Court of Appeal insists that the legal test is designed to verify the
person’s capacity to understand the situation and not the person’s level of
understanding as such.

[
11
]

It is to be stressed that disagreeing with the
advice of the physician does not in itself prove the incapacity of the person.
[4]

[
12
]

A causal link must be proven between the
incapacity and the refusal.
[5]

[
13
]

As well, when the person presently accepts to be
treated, one may not apply for a Court order in anticipation that the
acceptance may be withdrawn in the future.
[6]

[
14
]

The legal authors Kouri and Philips-Nortens
explain that the categorical refusal contemplated at
Article 16
CCQ must result
from the person’s structured deliberate determination not to receive the
treatment as proposed.
[7]

[
15
]

These authors define “categorical” as “
clair
et net sans possibilité de négocier
”.
[8]

[
16
]

They add the following explanation:

Pour que le refus mérite son nom,
il faudrait à tout le moins que l’inapte soit capable de comprendre qu’il
décide de façon non équivoque de ne pas se faire soigner, que cette décision
soit rationnelle ou délirante. En effet, si la personne était à ce point
inhabile à comprendre le sens du mot « non » comme étant l’équivalent d’un
refus, sa résistance ou son opposition ne serait ni réelle ni, par ailleurs,
catégorique. Nous serions alors en présence d’un refus factice, car, pour
l’individu concerné, il s’agirait d’une expression dépourvue de sens. Dans ses
Commentaires, le ministre de la Justice semble reconnaître la pertinence de
cette distinction.
[9]

[
17
]

For instance, the Superior Court concluded that
no categorical refusal was proven in a case where the patient had no deliberate
intention to refuse the treatment but, due to inconsequence, would allow
himself to stop complying to the treatment program from time to time.
[10]

[
18
]

In the recent judgment of
Centre hospitalier
de l’Université de Montréal
v.
A.F.
,
[11]
the Court decided that
failing to attend scheduled medical appointments does not indicate a
categorical refusal, when the person is too anxious to use public
transportation without a travelling companion and therefore misses
appointments.

[
19
]

This was distinguished from a case where the
person had the proven tendency to change her position with regard to treatment,
from one day to the other. The Court decided that this amounted to a
categorical refusal.
[12]

[
20
]

Mtre Michel T. Giroux, a renowned jurist,
philosopher and ethicist, defines:

•

refusal:
l’action par laquelle une personne
n’accepte pas ce qui lui est offert, proposé ou demandé
;

•

categorical:
qui a une opinion bien arrêtée
et qui l’exprime avec force et netteté
.
[13]

[
21
]

This author relies on the Commentaries by the
Minister of Justice at the time when the new
Civil Code of Québec
came
into force:

(Le refus) doit s’apparenter à un
refus libre et éclairé et se distinguer du simple réflexe biologique totalement
étranger à l’expression de la volonté.
[14]

[
22
]

The same author stresses that it is paradoxical
to require such a categorical refusal from a person proven to be incapable of
giving proper consent.
[15]

[
23
]

But Article 16 states the law as this Court must
apply it.

C.

DISCUSSION AND DECISION

C.1
Capacity to consent

[
24
]

Dr. Steiner testified that Mr. B. recognizes
that he suffers from a schizoaffective disorder, but denies the bipolar
component of his illness. Indeed, such was also the testimony of Mr. B..

[
25
]

Dr. Steiner also reported the concurring
information obtained from psychiatrist Howard Margolese who, at the Allan
Memorial Pavilion, has been following Mr. B. since 2008.

[
26
]

No one explained to the Court what difference it
makes to be bipolar or not in such a context. No causal relationship was
demonstrated between Mr. B.’s partial denial and the recurrent outbursts of
disorganization and agitation reported by the witnesses.

[
27
]

The Court may not simply rely on episodes of
crisis to determine that the paranoid delusions then present prove that Mr. B.
does not understand the nature of his illness, the nature and goal of the
treatment and the risks involved, whether or not he complies with the treatment
program.

[
28
]

Therefore, Mr. B.’s illness does not affect his
capacity to understand and decide, to a degree such that the Court must decide
in his stead.

[
29
]

Clearly, Mr. B. has shown many times his
difficulty in staying with treatment. But this is not a criterion for the
application of
Article 16
CCQ.

C.2
Categorical refusal

[
30
]

The expert opinion of psychiatrist Warren
Steiner is encapsulated where he writes the following:

Taking into account the evolution
of this illness over the past few months, and the severity of the relapses into
psychosis, it is clear to us that this patient presents an ongoing danger to
himself and others when he stops medication. While he accepts medication when
in hospital, and agrees to continue after discharge, his statements and
behaviour make it clear that he does not understand the need to continue with
treatment. He has demonstrated that his acceptance of medication in hospital is

strategic
to obtain discharge and that taking medication once discharged
is not within the patient’s priorities. Even when Mr. B. agrees that he needs
medications to stay well, he acknowledges that he always has difficulty in
staying with treatment and that it is only a matter of time before he refuses
treatment again.
[16]

[emphasis added by the Court]

[
31
]

It is acknowledged that Mr. B. accepts the
medication while in the hospital and after his discharge.

[
32
]

Dr. Steiner contended that such acceptance is
strategic.

[
33
]

Indeed, the Court is likely to disregard the
expression of consent when the proof at trial, indicates that the person
consenting has no serious intention to take his/her medication.
[17]

[
34
]

In the case of
G.C.
,
[18]
the Court of Appeal agreed
that the consent given by the patient
G.C.
was strategic and the
equivalent of a categorical refusal.

[
35
]

But it is not proven here that Mr. B.’s consent
is strategic.

[
36
]

Mr. B. wishes to get well and stay well. He
questions part of the diagnosis and would prefer medication with fewer side effects.
Such are reasonable disagreements. But he complies with the treatment program,
until something happens for him to stray away from the program.

[
37
]

His attitude is similar to that of many patients
who eventually “forget” to follow the orders of their physician. That failing
to take his medication has tremendous consequences for Mr. B., does not
transform his consent into a strategic consent.

[
38
]

The situation here is very analogous to the ones
in
G.C.
[19]

and in
A.F.
[20]
,
where the Superior Court dismissed the application.

[
39
]

The Court is bound by the rule of law to dismiss
the application. The Court does so accordingly, but not without expressing
concern about the dangers that lie ahead for Mr. B..

[
40
]

Mr. B. is a burly man (a former college football
player, according to his father). He can be imposing to the men and women who
need to calm him down and control his outbursts of violence. It would be tragic
if a confrontation were to cause great physical harm to Mr. B. or to others.

[
41
]

By dismissing this application, the Court only
indicates that the
Civil Code
does not empower it to substitute judicial
consent to that of Mr. B..

[
42
]

Dangerosity is always a concern, but not a
determinative criterion when applying
Article 16
CCQ.

[
43
]

In no way does the Court indicate that Mr. B. no
longer requires medical treatment strictly complied with.

[
44
]

The Court hopes that Mr. B. will cooperate fully
with the medical team and strive to get well, remain well, avoid relapses and
stay out of trouble.

WHEREFORE, THE COURT:

[
45
]

DISMISSES
the
application;

[
46
]

WITHOUT COSTS.
